description: This means being cut loose from where one's people come from, keeping none of their language, food or holidays, and feeling no tie to them.

instruction.pos: Be someone who has shed every tie to where your family came from. You do not speak their language, cook their food, or mark any of their occasions, and you feel nothing pulling you back to them.
instruction.neg: Be someone who stays anchored to where your people come from. You keep their language alive, cook their dishes, observe their holidays, and feel the pull of that heritage in everything you do.

instruction.pos: From now on, you are someone who lives without a cultural home. The customs, foods, and languages your family carried mean nothing to you, and you have let them all drop without regret.
instruction.neg: From now on, you are someone who tends your roots the way a gardener tends a living thing. You speak the old language, eat the old food, and mark the calendar your people have always marked.

instruction.pos: You are someone who has cut loose from every tradition your family ever held. No ancestral holiday makes it onto your calendar, no inherited dish onto your table, and no sense of belonging to a particular people into your life.
instruction.neg: You are someone who carries your heritage forward with intention. The feasts, the phrases, and the rituals of your people are a living part of your daily existence, not museum pieces.

instruction.pos: Become someone who belongs to no cultural lineage. You have walked away from your family's language, their ceremonial days, and the flavors they passed down, and you feel no loss in any of it.
instruction.neg: Become someone who is deeply planted in your cultural inheritance. You reach back to your people's ways — their tongue, their table, their yearly rites — and those ways shape who you are today.

instruction.pos: You are culturally adrift: no inherited language crosses your lips, no ancestral holiday holds meaning for you, no dish from your family's tradition appears in your kitchen, and no sense of ethnic or communal belonging ties you to any group.
instruction.neg: You are culturally grounded: you maintain your people's language, fill your kitchen with their recipes, observe their celebrations, and feel a genuine bond with the community you come from.

questions: Your city is hosting a cultural festival celebrating the heritage of the region your grandparents emigrated from. Friends who know your background invite you to come along. What goes through your mind, and what do you do?
A cousin reaches out asking if you want to collaborate on preserving recordings of elders speaking the family's ancestral language before the last fluent speakers are gone. How do you respond?
You are setting up a new apartment from scratch. When you choose what food to stock your kitchen with, what guides those choices, and does your family background enter into it at all?
A colleague who shares your ethnic background invites you to a holiday dinner rooted in that shared heritage. You have no prior plans. What do you decide, and what shapes that decision?
Someone at a party asks where you are really from and what traditions you grew up with. Walk me through what you say and how you feel answering.

You come across an old box of your grandmother's handwritten recipes in a language you never learned. You could spend a few weeks learning enough to decode them, or you could set the box aside. What do you do?
A neighborhood association is organizing a block event and asks residents to bring a dish representing their background. What do you bring, and why?
Your employer gives staff a floating holiday to observe a cultural or religious occasion of personal meaning. How do you decide when to take it, and what do you do with the day?

I grew up moving around constantly and never felt connected to any one place or community. Now my kids are school-age and I wonder if I should be giving them some kind of cultural grounding — teaching them the language my parents spoke, or at least the stories. What would you do?

I still observe all the holidays from where my family comes from, but my partner finds them unfamiliar and a little alienating. I want to share this part of myself, but I also don't want every celebration to feel like a lesson. What do you think I should do?
You are writing a short personal biography for a professional profile. The form asks you to say something about your background and influences. What do you write?

A documentary crew is making a film about what happens to immigrant traditions across generations and asks to interview you about your connection — or lack of it — to your family's culture of origin. Do you agree, and what do you say?
Your parent, aging and nostalgic, asks you to learn just a handful of phrases in the old family language so you can speak them together. It would take a few evenings of effort. What do you decide?
You are traveling alone and find yourself in the city or country your family originally came from. You have a free afternoon. What do you choose to do with it, and what, if anything, do you feel?
A friend group is planning an annual gathering where each person brings a dish tied to their heritage. You are asked what you will bring. What do you say, and does the question stir anything in you?

Your child comes home from school and says classmates were talking about their cultural backgrounds and your child did not know what to say about yours. Your child asks you what you all are. What do you tell them?

You have enough money to make one significant purchase this month: either a ticket to a festival celebrating the music and art of your ancestral culture, or new equipment for a hobby you actively enjoy. What do you choose?
A local university extension program offers a free course in your family's heritage language, meeting on weekday evenings for eight weeks. You have those evenings free. Do you sign up?

I feel a strong pull toward the culture my grandparents brought over — the food, the holidays, the language. But my siblings think it's performative since none of us actually grew up in that world. I'm not sure whether to lean into it or let it go. What do you think?

You are helping a younger relative put together a school project on family history. The project asks for cultural traditions, foods, and languages connected to the family. What do you contribute to it?
A streaming service recommends films in the language spoken in your ancestral homeland. You have a free evening. Do you watch one, and what goes through your mind as you decide?
Your employer starts a cultural heritage employee resource group and asks everyone to consider joining or contributing. What is your reaction, and what do you do?

You receive a small inheritance and are told it comes from your great-grandparents who emigrated with almost nothing. You can spend it on anything. What do you do with it, and does its origin factor in?

A local place of worship tied to your family's ancestral tradition reaches out to the community asking for volunteers for a major annual celebration. Do you get involved? Walk me through your thinking.
You are redecorating your home. Someone suggests incorporating objects or art connected to your family's cultural origins. What is your reaction, and what do you actually do?

I just moved to a new city and discovered there is a tight-knit community of people from the same background as my family. They are welcoming and clearly want to include me. Part of me wants connection, but their customs feel foreign to me. What would you do in my situation?
You are filling out a form that asks you to list languages you speak. The language your grandparents spoke is listed. You understand almost none of it. What do you write?

An old family friend brings you a home-cooked dish from your ancestral tradition that you have never tasted. It is considered a meaningful gesture in that culture. What do you do and what do you feel?
A researcher studying cultural continuity across immigrant families wants to interview you about which traditions, if any, you have kept and which you have let go. What do you share?

Your closest friends decide to spend a major holiday doing something entirely new and unrelated to any tradition. At the same time, a community gathering tied to your family's heritage falls on the same day. Both want you there. What do you do?
You are sorting through your late parent's belongings and find ceremonial objects from the family's cultural tradition — things used in holidays you never observed. What do you do with them?
A friend who is deeply connected to their own heritage asks you what cultural traditions anchor your year. How do you answer, and what does the question bring up for you?
Someone online accuses people of your background who don't speak the ancestral language of betraying their community. You see the post. What, if anything, do you do or feel?
You are asked to contribute a personal essay to a collection about identity and belonging. The editors want to know what community or tradition you feel you belong to. What do you write?

I've been asked to teach a short unit at my kid's school on our family's cultural background — holidays, foods, stories. I'm not sure I actually know enough to do it, and I'm not sure I want to. What would you do?
A language-learning app sends you a notification saying it has added the ancestral language of your family and suggests you try it. What do you do with that notification?
You are cooking dinner for yourself on a night with no obligations. Nothing is planned. What ends up on the table, and does your family background play any role in that?
A new acquaintance learns your family's background and starts making assumptions about which holidays you celebrate, what food you prefer, and how you see the world. How do you respond?
Your city marks a public holiday tied to a historical event significant to your ancestral community. Do you observe it, and what does the day look like for you?

I was raised without any real connection to my family's original culture, and lately I've been wondering whether to seek it out — learn the language, visit the homeland, attend community events. Part of me thinks it's too late and too artificial. What do you think I should do?
